title: Study in Italy Without IELTS 2027: MOI, Interviews and the B2 Reality
seoTitle: Study in Italy Without IELTS 2027: MOI Rules & Evidence
seoDescription: Can you study in Italy without IELTS in 2027? How Italian universities treat MOI letters, interviews and B2 evidence — plus the DSU grant and visa funds rules.
intro: Italy has no national IELTS rule — programmes decide. How MOI letters, interviews and B2 evidence actually work, and how to apply around them.
description: How to study in Italy without IELTS in 2027: MOI acceptance, interviews, DSU funding and visa funds explained.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: How Italian universities treat MOI letters and interviews instead of IELTS — and how to apply around them.
content:
Italy is quietly becoming the best "without IELTS" destination in continental Europe — not because Italian universities waive English, but because of how their system is built. Admissions are programme-by-programme, hundreds of English-taught degrees exist at public tuition rates, several universities substitute an interview or an MOI letter for a certificate, and the country’s need-based DSU grant can cover everything else. There is no national IELTS rule to fight — which means the outcome depends almost entirely on picking the right programmes and asking the right questions before applying.

What actually replaces IELTS in Italy

Italian universities declare a language level — usually B2 — and then decide case by case what proves it. In practice, five evidence types recur, and their acceptance varies more by university than by programme ranking:

[[chart:italy-evidence-cost]]
Evidence typeHow Italian universities treat it
Medium of Instruction (MOI) letterAccepted by a meaningful share of English-taught programmes, especially where the university runs its own interview; never guaranteed — ask the programme first.
Previous degree taught in EnglishThe strongest exemption case; many universities waive certificates outright when the bachelor’s was English-taught.
B2-level certificate from your home universitySome universities accept a university-issued English-level statement instead of IELTS.
Online interviewCommon substitute at Italian universities: a short spoken English interview replaces the certificate.
Duolingo / Linguaskill / PTEAcceptance varies widely; Duolingo is the least uniformly accepted of the three.

The reliable move is identical to our UK advice in the UK MOI guide: shortlist first, then email the programme’s admissions contact with one question — "is a Medium of Instruction letter from [your university] accepted as English evidence?" — and keep the written answer with your application file.

Why Italy pairs so well with the MOI route

Three structural reasons. First, public tuition is low and waivable: fees scale with family income (ISEE), and DSU grant winners study tuition-free — our DSU guide covers the €7,000-plus annual grant and its June-September 2027 windows. Second, interviews are normal: Italian admissions offices already run spoken assessments for restricted-access programmes, so substituting one for a certificate is administratively natural. Third, Erasmus Mundus programmes hosted in Italy — earthen architecture, green finance, climate change and territorial development, among others — admit through consortia where English evidence rules are written per programme and sometimes friendlier than national norms.

The English-taught landscape you are choosing from

Italy now runs hundreds of degree programmes entirely in English across its public universities — engineering at Milan and Turin, economics at Bologna, agriculture and food science at Bologna and Padua, public health and data science across the north — at public tuition that scales down to a few hundred euros a year once the ISEE income assessment is applied. Private institutions (Bocconi, the Bologna Business School ecosystem) charge real fees but carry their own merit waivers. For doctoral applicants, funded positions cluster around the same northern research hubs, and Italy-hosted Erasmus Mundus master’s programmes add two-country (often three-country) degrees on top. The point is not that Italy lacks options without IELTS — it is that the options are numerous enough that programme-level English policies, not country folklore, should drive your shortlist.

Universitaly, the national portal, sits at the centre of it all: pre-enrolment there initiates the visa paperwork and connects your identity, qualification and chosen programme in one record. Filing it early — even before final decisions — is free and keeps every later step on schedule.

Where applicants go wrong

  • Assuming "B2 required" means "IELTS required". The level is fixed; the evidence often is not. One email can save a €250 test.
  • Applying to the university but not the regional agency. DSU money lives with sixteen separate regional bodies, each with its own window — the single most common and most expensive omission.
  • Ignoring the visa funds rule. The type-D visa needs roughly €10,179.85 in traceable funds regardless of scholarships, and a DSU application does not count towards it — plan family funds for year one.
  • Missing pre-enrolment on Universitaly. The national pre-enrolment portal starts the visa process; it runs alongside, not after, your programme application.

The timeline that works

Italian calls for 2027 entry open in waves: some university windows run November-February, others stretch to spring; DSU applications follow in June-September 2027; pre-enrolment and visa steps occupy the summer. Sequence it as: shortlist in November, English-evidence emails in December, applications January-February, DSU documents (apostilles and translations) prepared in spring so the summer window costs you nothing. The 12-month application timeline maps the whole year.

The live Italian listings below — doctoral fellowships and Italy-hosted Erasmus Mundus programmes — are the kind of funded places where the MOI conversation is worth starting this month.
